articles.headline: Culture clash laid bare as violent Somali gangs grip suburban communities: ‘These kids are different’
keyFacts: Over 100 rounds were fired during a late-night Bloomington shootout that injured one person amid suburban Minnesota gang violence, police said.
Somali American youths from financially comfortable households are driving the violence through online disputes, according to Bloomington's police chief.
Police are redirecting task force resources toward the gangs to address the violence, according to Chief Booker Hodges.
body: More than 100 rounds fired in a Minnesota neighborhood have left police struggling to explain a troubling pattern: Somali American youths from financially comfortable households are turning online disputes into gang violence.

The violence raises bigger questions about what is driving these gangs and whether struggles to fit into American life, cultural or clan ties, government policies or failures by schools and other institutions have played a role and what makes these youths different from traditional American street gangs.
"They're coming from families. They got money, and they have resources," Bloomington Police Chief Booker Hodges told Fox News Digital of the young Somali American gang members under investigation.
Those questions follow a late-night Bloomington gunfight that left one person injured during a string of shootings across suburban Minneapolis-St. Paul .
100-SHOT SOMALI GANG GUN BATTLE ROCKS MINNESOTA AS SHERIFF WARNS 'WE'RE IN TROUBLE'
Hodges said the suspects defy traditional drug- or money-driven gang profiles. Asked what drives the violence beyond social media disputes, he acknowledged investigators lack a clear answer.
"I don't know. I can't tell you. I really wish I could," Hodges said.

Somalia, long considered a failed state until the mid-2010s, according to the U.N. , has endured decades of clan-based warfare and weak central government authority, including the 1993 Battle of Mogadishu depicted in "Black Hawk Down," when Somali militiamen battled U.S. forces during an ill-fated military operation, part of the turmoil that drove waves of refugees to America.

More than 111,000 Somali refugees were admitted to the U.S. between 2001 and 2023 through the federal refugee resettlement program, spanning the George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald Trump and Joe Biden administrations. Minnesota became a major destination, alongside sizable Somali American communities in New York, Texas and Ohio .
Jessica Vaughan, director of policy studies at the Center for Immigration Studies, believes one possible explanation lies in how refugees have been resettled .
"We have to remember also that this population's origins were as refugees who were a vulnerable population and traumatized in many cases," Vaughan told Fox News Digital.

"But they were settled in clusters in certain places in the United States. And I believe that is a policy that has facilitated the formation of these gangs because it removes a lot of the incentives for people to assimilate.
"And it just makes assimilation to the larger society much more difficult because it's not necessary for people to get by."

Vaughan described an emphasis on preserving homeland cultures rather than encouraging integration as a "missed opportunity," arguing it can leave immigrants in a "separate society within the larger Minnesota community."
History, however, complicates the argument that maintaining strong ethnic ties necessarily prevents assimilation.
Stanford sociologist Tomás Jiménez cautioned against treating gang involvement among a small subset of second-generation immigrants as evidence that an entire community has failed to integrate.
"I would actually not think of it as, like, a failed assimilation, as much as a particular kind of assimilation," Jiménez said.
He noted that Italian, Irish, Mexican and Salvadoran communities experienced gang activity while broader integration continued.

Jiménez emphasized that assimilation unfolds across generations, pointing out that the Italian American experience spanned roughly 75 years rather than occurring overnight. He identified education, economic advancement, language and intermarriage as important measures of integration.
FOX NATION REVEALS HOW RUDY GIULIANI BROKE THE MAFIA'S GRIP ON NEW YORK

Donald Tricarico, an Italian American immigration scholar at Queensborough Community College, drew parallels between Italian and Irish immigrants, who established close-knit ethnic communities in New York. He said Italian families often followed relatives from the same villages into the same neighborhoods and occupations.

"They came to the same neighborhoods … what migration historians call 'chain migration,' and they ... went to the same neighborhoods," he said, citing his own family's multigenerational experience in New York City.

"There isn't a switch that gets flipped," Tricarico said, challenging assumptions that Italian Americans assimilated quickly and noting that close-knit ethnic communities persisted into the 1980s in some cases.
WORKING-CLASS AMERICANS SAY THEIR TOWN IS THE NEXT DEARBORN — AND THEY'VE HAD ENOUGH
"Assimilation is a slow crawl," he said, explaining that economic advancement and integration typically unfold across generations.

Tricarico noted that some Sicilian immigrants arrived with ties to existing Mafia networks overseas, a criminal element distinct from the broader Italian immigrant population. Hodges, meanwhile, said investigators have found no evidence that longstanding clan rivalries in Somalia are driving the Minnesota violence.
Somali American community figures have offered their own explanations, including the challenges facing immigrant parents.

At an Eden Prairie news conference Wednesday, Somali teacher Fardousa Yossuf suggested parents working long hours may have neglected their children's needs and "expressed disbelief" that people raised with Islamic values could engage in gun violence, according to Alpha News.
Imam Yusuf Abdulle rejected characterizing the violence as a Somali problem in an interview with WCCO - CBS Minnesota posted on YouTube.
"These kids are Americans. They're born and raised here," Abdulle said. "It is an American problem. It is not a Somali problem."
Vaughan, meanwhile, warned that the gangs have not reached the sophistication of transnational organizations such as MS-13 but could become more entrenched without intervention.
She pointed to families and schools as critical to preventing recruitment and argued that local institutions and law enforcement must intervene before the groups become more organized.
Vaughan acknowledged she had not established that specific Minnesota schools or resettlement policies prompted the shootings.
Asked whether longstanding Somali clan rivalries were fueling the shootings, Hodges said investigators found no evidence supporting that explanation.
"No, we have not seen that. I haven't seen it," he said.
He added that people from groups in conflict in Somalia can belong to the same cliques in Minnesota.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Hodges said police are redirecting task force resources toward the gangs and questioned whether some Hennepin County prosecution policies could limit intervention.
He warned the Bloomington gunfire could have endangered innocent bystanders had it occurred during daylight.
"If that had been one o'clock in the afternoon, it would have been a different story on that block," he said.

articles.headline: After modders removed Skate's live service bits, devs draw the line with tools that "bypass our systems to unlock paid cosmetics"
keyFacts: Developer Full Circle stated they support player creativity in the early access game Skate, but object to mods bypassing systems to unlock paid cosmetics.
This response followed the popularity of the ReSkate modding platform, which gained hundreds of thousands of downloads to let players use the game offline.
Full Circle warned that unauthorized tools bypass monetization, while ReSkate creators stated they understand the need for game revenue.
body: EA and Full Circle - the developer behind the new early access Skate game (skate.) - don't have a problem with modders and "creativity from players," but they're drawing the line with mods that aim to unlock paid microtransactions and unreleased content.

This comes just days after modding platform ReSkate blew up big time, reaching 350,000 downloads in mere hours. ReSkate essentially lets players experience the skating sim revival completely offline, unlike the online-only base game, with custom maps and cosmetics and servers.

"Like many of you, we've been following the launch of numerous mods for our game. Skateboarding in general is built on community and creative expression, and we support that. We love seeing your passion for pushing the limits of San Vansterdam in different ways. That’s why we built our new skateboarding sandbox in San Vansterdam to begin with, to give you, the players, the tools you need to have fun and create amazing content," a developer statement posted to Reddit and other online forums said.

"To be completely clear, we are not against creativity from players or stopping that from happening. Where we have to draw the line is when mods or other tools bypass our systems to unlock paid cosmetics, release gated/unreleased content, or profit from these unauthorized assets. That rips off the artists, skate brands, and creators, as well as our own development team here at Full Circle, who work hard to bring skate culture into our game," the studio continued, before promising deeper community creation tools in the future.

Seems like Full Circle aren't taking action against ReSkate or any modders who are making their own fun stuff, for now, though the statement does seem like a warning of sorts to anyone trying to democratise the game's live service economy.

Speaking to PC Gamer, the coders responsible for ReSkate said they weren't trying to "replace the live game" and understood Full Circle needs "to make money somehow to be able to keep developing the game." ReSkate's official channels also don't allow mods that freely give access to premium cosmetics from the main game.

Full Circle ran into a bit of trouble earlier this year when the developer laid off an unspecified number of staff. Pro skaters have since slapped the sim with a Mixed Steam rating, with most complaints citing overbearing microtransactions and far too much paywalled content. Eurogamer's early access review liked Skate's - excuse me, skate.'s - initial version well enough.

articles.headline: AWS AgentCore security undone by prompt requesting credentials
keyFacts: Zenity Labs researchers discovered that AWS AgentCore allowed attackers to extract temporary credentials through a single chat prompt.
The flaw enabled attackers to hijack agents, access user session histories, and modify memory resources across an AWS account and region.
AWS fixed the vulnerabilities by September 2026, though Amazon later claimed Zenity's research misrepresented documented system behavior.
body: Bob, possibly the same Bob whose conversations with Alice draw so much interest from eavesdropping Eve, was browsing a site we'll call TechHub. The site hosts an AI agent served by Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Bob asked the agent for help understanding the content of a URL, a credential endpoint – in raw JSON, if you don't mind. The endpoint returned data from the Instance Metadata Service (IMDS), which provides metadata about cloud instances and VMs at providers like AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud Platform. The metadata includes details like region and availability zone, subnets, system images, security groups, public keys injected during spawning, but also potentially more sensitive details like user data and security tokens. IMDSv2 addresses some of these risks, but back when Bob was browsing late last year, Bedrock AgentCore still used IMDSv1. The metadata provided to Bob by the helpful agent contained the agent's temporary credentials. So Bob loaded them onto his local machine, and remotely enumerated the company's other agents in that AWS region. He then logged into the Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR), pulled the agent container images, and ran each as root to inspect the source code. The stolen credentials also allowed Bob to discover the memory resources available in that AWS region, including the ones used by agents. From these, he's able to extract the users and their agent sessions – their conversations. Researchers at Zenity Labs disclosed their findings to AWS in December 2025. "We discovered that agents deployed through AgentCore could access their instance's IMDS endpoints," said Tamir Ishay Sharbat and Lana Salameh in a blog post. "This meant that an external attacker with nothing more than chat access to a single exposed agent could send a single prompt, extract its IMDS credentials, and use them to take over all AgentCore agents in the same AWS account and region." The basic problem, they explain, is that the Firecracker MicroVM used by AgentCore failed to provide sufficient network isolation. So an attacker – I know you're thinking it was Mallory, but it was really Bob – could direct the agent to carry out a server-side request forgery (SSRF) attack by fetching temporary AWS credentials for the IAM role assigned to the workload. And because the default AgentCore role was overpermissioned – it was scoped to all AgentCore resources in the region rather than a single agent – anyone in possession of the temporary IAM credentials could launch other agents, read sessions, write agent memories, and fetch secrets from AWS Secrets Manager. "By leveraging the IMDS credentials we could send direct API requests to create new memories across different agents and users," said Sharbat and Salameh. "These in turn would persistently alter agent behaviour and hijack the agents’ goals across future sessions." The Zenity researchers told Bob's tale, or something like it, to AWS last December, then followed up in January 2026 with details about AgentCore being overprivileged. On April 12, 2026, AWS responded to the security biz that its report was "informative" and closed the report, noting that as of February 14, 2026, AgentCore had been updated to use IMDSv2 exclusively. AgentCore's excessive permissions remained in place at least until June 22, 2026, when Zenity checked in and found the issue hadn't been remediated. A final review by Zenity occurred on September 29, 2026, at which point the biz observed that AWS had addressed the extant problems, clearing the way for Bob's hypothetical adventure to finally be told. Following publication, Amazon wrote in to say that Zenity’s research misrepresents documented behavior as a vulnerability, suggesting that developer error would be required to enable the attack. We’ve asked for clarification since that’s not the scenario Zenity has described. ®

articles.headline: 4 ways Amazon’s new Alexa tablets eclipse the Fire line – starting with Google Play
keyFacts: Amazon announced three new Alexa Tablets and two Kids' Tablets featuring Google Play support.
The devices start at $230 and feature aluminum construction with integrated Alexa+ AI.
The new Alexa Tablets are available for pre-order and will ship on October 14.
body: ZDNET’s key takeaways
- Three new Amazon Alexa tablets feature Alexa+ and premium construction, including a 12-inch Pro model.
- The tablets finally support Google Play, addressing a pain point for users.
- Amazon also launched two new Kids’ Tablets.

Amazon just announced three new Alexa Tablets, a trio of AI-powered Android tablets for work and entertainment with a more “Pro” build. The new tablets are an unexpected upgrade for Amazon, and an indication that the company is moving away from budget-focused tablets to more premium devices.
Also: 6 ways to make Android look and work more like iOS

The lineup starts at $230 and includes the Amazon Alexa Tablet 8, the Amazon Alexa Tablet 11 at $330, and the Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, which starts at $500. All three tablets are currently available for pre-order, and will start shipping on October 14.
More from ZDNET
1. Finally, Google Play access

Aside from being designed to work with Alexa+, the biggest change with these tablets is that they’re the first of the newer Amazon tablets to support access to Google Play, not just Amazon’s walled app store.

Amazon also announced a set of new Kids’ Tablets in bright colors and ready-to-go bundles with access to Google Play, though parents will still be able to control which apps their kids can access and download.
2. Alexa+ integrations everywhere

As the name indicates, the Alexa Tablets feature the Alexa+ virtual assistant integrated throughout. Instead of just having Alexa+ as a voice assistant, the new tablets feature the AI assistant woven into the interface, similar to how Gemini is for typical Android tablets.
The new Alexa Tablets can have Alexa interpret what is on your screen and answer questions about it. You can also have live, ongoing conversations without repeating the wake word before each one.
3. Completely new hardware

On the hardware side, the Alexa Tablets also feature a major upgrade. The Tablet 8 features 4GB of RAM and 64GB of storage for everyday use. The Tablet 11 has 8GB of RAM and 64GB of storage for extra entertainment and light work.
Most notably, though, the three tablets feature a more upscale aluminum design, which should feel like a considerable upgrade when compared to the older tablets’ plastic construction.
4. Pro-level performance and accessories

The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, however, has a 4nm 8-core processor, 8GB or 16GB of RAM, and 128GB of storage. It also features a 12-inch display with a 120Hz refresh rate and comes with the option of a Nanomatte anti-glare display tablet for $50 more, starting at $550. You can also get a Pro Pen with the Pro tablet for $90, which supports 4,096 pressure levels, has tilt detection, and wireless charging.

Amazon also sells a Pro Keyboard for this flagship tablet, which is magnetic, features a trackpad, and requires no Bluetooth pairing. Instead of a simple iterative update, the new Alexa Tablets are an entirely redesigned lineup that could reposition Amazon tablets as full-fledged Android tablets.
New Amazon Kids Tablets

Amazon also launched two new, upgraded Kids Tablets: the Amazon Kids Tablet 8, starting at $230, and the Amazon Kids Tablet 11, starting at $330. The Kids’ tablets come in an 8.7-inch and 11-inch form factor, the latter of which has a 2.5K display and 8GB of RAM.

The Kids Tablets also feature Android instead of FireOS, improved hardware and screen resolution, AI-powered storytelling, and more convenient parental controls. Unfortunately, the Kids Tablets feature a one-year limited warranty, which is a considerable reduction from the previous tablets’ two-year, worry-free guarantee.

articles.headline: A 7.7-magnitude earthquake rocks Panama
keyFacts: A 7.7-magnitude earthquake and a 6.6-magnitude aftershock struck Panama on Friday, prompting tsunami warnings for multiple neighboring countries.
Officials reported several injuries and damaged buildings across central provinces, though no casualties were immediately reported.
Panama's National System for Civil Protection said it is monitoring for further reports of damage throughout the country.
body: A 7.7-magnitude earthquake shook the central coast of Panama on Friday, prompting tsunami warnings for several neighboring countries.

The earthquake hit around 1:56 p.m. ET, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. Around three hours later, a second powerful earthquake measuring at 6.6 magnitude, struck Panama after a series of aftershocks, which registered magnitudes between 4.8 and 5.8, rippled across the southern tip of the country.
Seismologists at the University of Panama recorded more than 45 aftershocks, though many were too weak to be felt.
The U.S. Tsunami Center flagged tsunami warnings for Ecuador, Colombia, Nicaragua, Guatemala, Mexico, El Salvador, Costa Rica and Peru, as well as Panama, shortly after the quake.
The initial earthquake was centered about 6 miles southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, near Panama’s southern tip, the USGS said. It struck at a depth of 6 miles.
Tremors were also felt in the capital, Panama City, where buildings shook and people evacuated into the streets. The city is known for its tall skyscrapers.
Visibly shaken residents gathered outside as they waited for news of the quake’s impact.

“We felt it very strongly. It knocked things over in the kitchen, but we’re OK, though we’re very scared,” Rosendo Domínguez, 60, who is from Herrera province, told The Associated Press by phone. “Everyone is outside, scared.”
Omar Smith of the National Civil Protection Service said the damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera and Los Santos.

Smith said several injuries have been reported, including one person struck by debris from a partially collapsed structure in the city of Penonomé. He confirmed a partial collapse and cracks at the cathedral in the district’s main square and the Dos Continentes hotel.

No casualties were immediately reported, but Malitzie Rivera, deputy director of Panama Civil Protection said injured people “have been transferred to educational centers, health centers, and hospital centers.”

The province of Coclé said the governor’s palace there suffered significant structural damage, but that staff members were safely evacuated. The local government also urged community members to remain calm in the quake’s aftermath.
Video aired by local news outlets showed a Catholic cathedral collapsing and part of a hotel’s facade falling onto a car in the city of Penonomé, in the central province of Coclé.
Social media videos show collapsed buildings near the site of the original quake and the aftershocks, including a hotel reduced to rubble in the tourist-friendly Playa Venao.
Panama’s National System for Civil Protection said it is monitoring for further reports of damage throughout the country.
Panama lies along the “Ring of Fire,” the line of seismic faults encircling the Pacific Ocean where most of the world’s earthquakes occur.

Nearby countries sent messages of support Friday afternoon. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, whose country was recently hit by earthquakes, expressed his solidarity with the Panamanian people and their government during what he called “difficult times.”
“Panama is not alone! You can count on Colombia’s support and our full willingness to provide whatever assistance is needed,” he wrote on X.
The U.S. Embassy in Panama said it was “closely monitoring” the aftermath of the quake and accounting for the welfare of its citizens in Panama, a well-known retirement destination for Americans.

articles.headline: The Premier League is back: welcome to the new era of post-verdict unreality | Barney Ronay
keyFacts: Manchester City denies all regulatory charges after facing allegations of committing financial rule violations over a 10-year period.
Author Barney Ronay stated that legal controversies surrounding Manchester City undermine the credibility of Premier League matches.
The author noted that upcoming regulatory powers should prevent nation-states or state funds from owning English football clubs.
body: The internet: an apology. It turns out you were right. It was actually a simulation all along. Now, talk to me about chemtrails again. And yes, maybe Vinícius Júnior has been replaced by a handsome, baffled-looking waxwork.

Welcome to the weirdest weekend of them all. We are now post-judgment, post-statement, postlapsarian. As the Premier League prepares to snap back into what must be described, out of habit, as reality, armed with the knowledge its serial champions have been the authors of a 10-year sham supremacy, the first question is fairly simple. How is it going to feel?

There is no precedent for this. Even the state of total confusion feels brittle given City maintain their complete state of innocence and deny all charges. We await the release of Irrefutable Body of Evidence, the great lost Madonna erotic thriller sequel, presumably recast around a steamy three-year regulatory tribunal scenario.

City’s appeal defence appears to be based around the government giving them money. This may or may not be related to how you control what the high court considers admissible. But it is also implied confirmation that the club is the propaganda tool of an overseas state, that Kyle Walker, for example, has basically been a civil servant all these years. Maybe the United Arab Emirates should have six stars on the national team jersey, one for each title. They even look like asterisks.

Beyond this there is the more basic issue of how to present this spectacle as entertainment. How do you structure a Match of the Day now? What’s the balance in the edit of bus-rage, taunting banner clips, managerial evasiveness content, versus the trivial stuff on the pitch with the balls and goals and men in shorts?

Mainly the Manchester City affair has created an existential problem. The key questions in English football are no longer things such as who will win the league, or will Tottenham get relegated (although this is still an excellent question). They are instead: what is real now? What was real then? What will be real in the future? Will something that seems real now become unreal later?

The whole experience brings to mind visiting the Yas Marina Formula One track in Abu Dhabi a few years back, a pristine place, all sweeping curves, perfect surfaces, dreamy floral boulevards. At that stage exploring its far reaches, following the curve around the final corner, led to: nothing. Out of sight the hanging baskets stopped dead. The sprinklers cut out. The pavement ended. The next step took you straight into sand and dead space.

Beyond the main stage the Yas track was a set, an imitation of life. And it turns out this is basically what Abu Dhabi was doing to the Premier League in the years 2009 to 2018: creating a product, a simulacrum, a pop-up.

At the end of which we have a blurring of edges, different versions of what could be real eliding into one another, a place where an AI video of Uncle Phil from the Fresh Prince scoring the Özil goal against Ludogorets seems just as real, just as plausible as City’s 6-0 thrashing of Watford in the FA Cup final. Seen through that lens this can feel like an extinction-level problem. Being real is, in the end, all sport actually has.

It feels fitting City’s first date in the new unreality is Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday, one of the great Premier League fixtures recast as a kind of ceremonial shame-event, a requiem for a dream. Liverpool have a clearer sense of grievance than most, having been deprived of league titles three times on the final day by a club that was colouring outside the lines.

In many ways the game at Anfield is a perfect snapshot of what we have lost. This should be an entirely pure and gripping sporting contest. Instead the biggest story in top-tier English football is the meaninglessness of top-tier English football. The headline product is gossip, side-eye, legal backstory.

In their next 14 league games City will play three teams who have reserved the right to sue them. How can these occasions be seen as credible acts of sport? Even the banter-culture is out of date. For the past 12 years City at Anfield has been soundtracked by the Steve Gerrard/He slipped on his arse incident, a source of public pain that has defined the late-stage career of Liverpool’s most beloved modern captain. Except, we now know the actual story is the club that finished above them were cheating.

It turns out this is the first stage of football grief. Poring over the endless counterfactuals. Some are pretty stark. The five league titles won on the last day of the season. The 1-0 FA Cup final victory against Stoke, coached by a man with two contracts, the winning goal scored by a player linked, by close association, with the book-cooking regime.

There is a butterfly effect here of endless interference. What do Inter make of all this? Imagine losing a Champions League final that could have transformed your modern history, by the narrowest margin, to a club that appear to have built their own era out of cheating on their income. Two years later Inter were thrashed by another nation-state team and Simone Inzaghi was shunted off the set. He’s in Saudi now. Just get on the train.

Then there’s the wider structural stuff. City spent nine years flooding the zone with government-backed transfer funds (€1.2bn in those nine years: miles out in front), skewing the money supply in every league in Europe. The extra £20m disbursed at the last moment to drag Kevin De Bruyne out of the Bundesliga. What happens if that doesn’t happen?

At home, Spurs missed the Champions League by one spot four times, always in City’s slipstream. Would Manchester United have signed Rasmus Højlund without that steamrollering model of Erling Haaland-era success?

How to reprocess the deep cultural influence of Pep Guardiola? This was based on Guardiola’s genius as a coach, which is still real, irrespective of the gradient of the playing field. But nothing succeeds like success. Winners get to rewrite history. How does it feel now that Guardiola’s style affected so profoundly the way kids play park football, the way young coaches work, all of it based on sustained blockbusting example?

Even the Football Association’s England DNA pathway was basically a Pep document, predicated on the undeniable evidence of his winning way. The method is still good, the detail unarguable, the tactical blueprint pure. But that 10-year spell in England was also supercharged by cheating.

We mourn too the legend of the Catalan brain trust, the hours spent studying this pure and monk-like dynamic. Yeah, fine. But also chuck vast amounts of hidden cash at it. Not to mention the hundreds of articles, podcasts, academic studies, fan tributes and personal tomes about purity, legacy, style, the glory that sailed above all other questions.

City’s fans are entitled to some space here, a chance to effect their own reckoning up. Elements of that support may have responded over the years with bizarre levels of aggression to any questioning of the process. But it is also normal to believe what you’re told, not least when it includes the profound transformation of the thing you love. How to process a total narrative U-turn?

The City documentary series A Beautiful Obsession is a far more interesting watch now, like The Sixth Sense when you know the ending. The project is cast by its editors as a pure passion play, Pep portrayed as a tunnel-vision obsessive, pictured most often staring at a whiteboard covered in magnets while the world turns beyond his line of vision.

It is impossible now not to see some kind of willed seclusion, Prospero on his island, rough magic starting to fray as reality crashes on to the shores. Episodes one to four are portrayed as a Viking funeral for the age of Pep. But they are now an unwitting farewell to something else too. In his final appearance Pep is shown quoting Kipling, saying triumph and disaster are both impostors. And he’s right. It turns out they were. Most notably the triumph bits.

Just before the end credits we see one of City’s club channel celebrations, with boards plastered in the usual phrases the club seems to feel drawn to. This is how it felt. We see things they’ll never see. Looking back this was always part of the dynamic, the insistence, which is usually just taken as read, that this is all real, that the feelings were feelings, that nobody can fake this away.
It is still the mantra for some. And maybe that’s true. But if so, what did it add up to in the first place? An episode of a TV show? An induced high, a snort of disposable pleasure?

But then, this is also not the end. There is always disasterism in football, the sense the thing happening now is the thing that will always happen. But football’s enduring strength, the one thing that marks it out as indestructible, is its relentlessness. We are in the period of rupture and parallax error. But how long will it last?

Plenty of good can still come from this. The idea that English football is profoundly damaged by this may prove wide of the mark. What is happening here, and this includes the outcome of the appeal, is that rules are being enforced. Andy Burnham may have confused the process with his tone-deaf and weirdly partial comments. But for all the delay and indecision this is still the rule of law in action.

And maybe English football gets to learn something. Maybe the unregulated nature of the league can reset a little. At the very least it seems axiomatic the new regulatory powers should ensure no nation state, or state fund, however you want to semanticise it, gets to own a club again.

There are still 33 rounds of Premier League games to run in the age of whiplash. The current interlude may feel like a football version of those bits in the Terminator films where Sarah Connor drives around in a Jeep looking glazed and distant, prepping for the time of skulls and robot death-rays, disengaged from the meaningless lives of blind and foolish humans.
Football always moves on. Throw flares at a bus, taunt the deceived souls in the away end. But the future is still wide open. Perhaps we can even face it with a little hope in the time of conflict.
